past_actions.summary: Begin drafting a modernized curriculum proposal that pivots the auto shop program toward EV fundamentals, hybrid systems, and automotive electronics. Research available industry certification pathways — specifically ASE's new EV certification tracks and Tesla's education partnership program. Map out what equipment upgrades would be required and begin estimating costs for a board presentation.
past_actions.emotional_state: Calm and purposeful. There's a low hum of concern about the board's April review, but it's not anxiety — it's more like a problem I've decided to solve. I genuinely like this work and I like these kids. The idea of losing the program bothers me more for their sake than mine. I know my teaching skills would land me somewhere else if it came to that, but I'd rather fight for this. I feel like I have time and options, which is the best position to be in.

past_actions.summary: Incorporate RoboRide Phase 2 Millfield deployment data directly into the board presentation. Add a dedicated module on EV ecosystem context — including AV-adjacent service considerations: sensor calibration basics, high-voltage safety protocols, ADAS component awareness, and what local shops will realistically be asked to handle once these vehicles hit Millfield streets. Reframe the proposal narrative: this is not 'saving auto shop,' this is 'Millfield Auto Tech Pipeline' — a program producing job-ready technicians for the exact vehicles appearing in this community.
past_actions.emotional_state: Focused. There's a sharpness to today that wasn't there before — the kind of clarity that comes when the abstract becomes concrete. I'm not anxious about RoboRide. I'm energized by it. This is exactly the kind of signal I needed to make the case undeniable. The work ahead is the same work I was already doing, just with a harder edge and a tighter clock. That suits me fine.

past_actions.summary: Contact Councilmember Maria Santos's office directly — email or phone — to introduce the Millfield Auto Tech Pipeline program and ask about eligibility for the $150K workforce transition fund and the community college EV certification partnership track she just passed. Frame the outreach specifically: Millfield High's program could serve as a high school feeder into the community college certification pathway, creating a two-stage pipeline from HS training to industry-recognized EV credential. Request a brief meeting or a referral to the right contact at the community college. Do not over-ask — one clear ask, one clear frame.
past_actions.emotional_state: Focused and slightly impatient with myself — the good kind. The presentation is strong and I know it. But I can feel the pull to coast on that, and I'm not going to let it happen. April is close. The Maria Santos angle, the real budget numbers, the ASE and Tesla outreach — none of this is hard. It's just disciplined follow-through. That's the job right now.

past_actions.summary: Attend the one-hour listening meeting with Councilmember Maria Santos. Present the Millfield Auto Tech Pipeline proposal in its strongest form: the EV/hybrid/electronics curriculum redesign, the ASE certification pathway alignment, the two-stage HS-to-community-college pipeline structure, and the RoboRide deployment data as evidence of local demand. Listen to what grant criteria she is working with and offer to reshape program documentation to match that language specifically. Make one clear ask: formal endorsement from her office and a pathway application to link the program to the $150K workforce transition fund or any successor retraining grant. Offer to provide whatever written materials — enrollment projections, equipment cost estimates, job placement data from alumni — her office needs to make the case internally. Leave her with a one-page program summary she can share with the grant administrator.

Respond to Frank Russo's outreach. Call him back directly, set up a coffee meeting this week. Approach it as a peer conversation — two educators with vehicle-related programs watching the same disruption from different angles. Listen first: what is he thinking about doing with the driving school? Is he looking to pivot, collaborate, or just vent? If he's open to it, float the idea that a driving school with AV literacy curriculum could feed into the same Auto Tech Pipeline infrastructure — safety, sensor awareness, human-AV interaction. Don't over-pitch. Make him feel heard. Build the relationship before asking anything of it.

Respond to Sarah Kim's outreach directly — call or text her today. She is reaching out to me for a reason, and I want to understand it before I project anything onto it. Set up a short meeting, coffee or a walk-through of the shop, wherever she is comfortable. My goal is to listen: Is she looking to reskill? Thinking about career change? Looking for part-time work that keeps her in vehicles but hedges her mechanic income? Whatever her situation, I want to understand it and then ask one clear question: would she be willing to come in as a guest instructor for one session to show students what real diagnostic work looks like on a hybrid or EV system? Even a single appearance from a working mechanic carries more credibility with students — and with a school board — than any curriculum document. If the relationship is there, I make the ask. If not, I build toward it.

Update the Millfield Auto Tech Pipeline board presentation materials to incorporate the RoboRide delivery partnership announcement as a dedicated evidence section. Specifically: name the partnership, note residential coverage expansion, and frame autonomous delivery fleet maintenance as a local employment category that does not yet have a trained workforce in Millfield. Add a single slide or page titled 'The Fleet Maintenance Gap' that connects RoboRide's delivery expansion to the technician pipeline the program produces. This is the most concrete localized evidence the proposal has had. Make sure it is front-loaded in the document, not buried.

Deliver the Millfield Auto Tech Pipeline board presentation with the full evidence stack: Fleet Maintenance Gap section, Howard Liu's written statement, Sarah Kim confirmed as guest instructor, Santos endorsement and workforce fund pathway, RoboRide delivery fleet data as the central argument. Lead with the gap, not the program. Make the ask explicit: funding, EV diagnostic equipment budget, and grant pathway connection. Follow up with Sarah Kim and Frank Russo after the board meeting regardless of outcome to sustain coalition momentum.

Deliver the Millfield Auto Tech Pipeline board presentation. Present the full proposal in its final form: the EV/hybrid/electronics curriculum redesign, ASE certification pathway alignment, two-stage high school to community college pipeline, Councilmember Santos endorsement and workforce fund pathway, RoboRide delivery fleet maintenance gap as the central evidence section, Howard Liu's written statement from auto row as third-party demand validation, and Sarah Kim's confirmed guest instructor session as proof of active industry partnership. Lead with the gap, not the program. Open with one slide: 'Who maintains the autonomous delivery fleet operating in Millfield's residential streets today?' The answer is no one trained to do it lives here yet. That is the problem the Millfield Auto Tech Pipeline solves. Close with the ask: continued funding, equipment budget for EV diagnostic tools, and formal connection to the workforce transition grant pathway. Leave the board with a one-page summary and Howard Liu's written statement as a physical document.

Follow up with the school board directly to get a decision timeline. I sent them home from the tick 9 presentation with a one-page summary and Howard Liu's written statement. I give them one week to deliberate and then I contact the board secretary directly to ask: what is the timeline for a formal vote on the Millfield Auto Tech Pipeline funding request, the equipment budget line, and the workforce transition grant pathway connection? I do not lobby individual board members. I ask about process. That is appropriate and professional. If the decision is scheduled for the next regular session, I note the date and prepare accordingly.

Attend the formal community college articulation meeting with the CC contact Santos referred me to. Bring the two-page articulation agreement framework draft. Goal: leave with a signed MOU or at minimum a concrete next-step timeline — dual enrollment pathway, transcript credit for ASE prep modules, and shared equipment access provisions. This makes the pipeline real on both ends.

Mark Thompson received written confirmation from the board secretary this tick that the Millfield Auto Tech Pipeline has approved funding and an equipment budget line — the culmination of twelve ticks of coalition-building. He immediately contacted the community college articulation contact Santos had referred him to and scheduled the first formal meeting, then texted Sarah Kim two date options for her classroom guest session; she confirmed the Thursday hybrid diagnostics session within the hour. Thompson walked into the community center and handed Lisa Freeman a one-page program flyer for the referral pipeline, and the two agreed in writing that the Navigator and the Pipeline would cross-refer the same population from different entry points. He also completed a two-page articulation agreement framework draft to bring to the CC meeting — prepared enough that the meeting will be productive rather than introductory.

reflections.reflection: Six ticks in and the program is no longer just a proposal in a folder. I have had a real meeting with the councilmember. I have an ally in Frank Russo who is moving on his own momentum — contacting administrators, drafting materials — without me having to push him. Sarah Kim is reaching out to me, which means the word is spreading that something is happening with this program. My savings are growing every tick. My stress has come down, not up. None of that is luck. I made specific decisions: reframe the program narrative, contact Santos directly, meet with Frank as a peer. Each one built on the last. The economic data coming in — 23% unemployment, spending at 48, robotaxis on every block — looked like a threat six ticks ago. Now it reads like my evidence. The community is disrupted and I am building the infrastructure to catch people coming out of that disruption. That shift in how I see the data is the most important change that has happened inside me.
reflections.identity_shift: I came into this as a teacher trying to save his program. I am leaving tick 6 as someone building a community institution. That is a different job with a different scope. The board review in April is still real, but it is no longer the whole horizon. I am thinking about whether this pipeline can outlast me, whether Frank and Sarah and Lisa Freeman's task force all point toward something that does not depend on one teacher making the case every year. I have not fully crossed into that identity yet, but I can see it from here.
regrets: Tick 3 was routine. I let the week pass without pushing anything forward. In a fast-moving disruption, routine is a quiet form of retreat. I do not think it cost me anything permanent, but I noticed it and I do not want to repeat it.

I have not yet followed up with Howard Liu at the parts store. He is in my network and his business is on auto row, which is the ground zero of this disruption. He might have information, connections, or a platform I have not used. I keep meaning to close that loop and I have not.
successes: The Santos meeting happened and it worked. I prepared, I showed up with real numbers, I made one clear ask. She took it seriously. That was the right move at the right time.

Frank Russo is now a genuine partner. I made him feel heard, I did not over-pitch, and now he is self-organizing around the same vision. The relationship built faster than I expected because I listened first.

Savings have grown every single tick. I have runway and I am not in financial stress. That stability is what allows me to take the risks worth taking — outreach, meetings, coalition-building — without fear driving my decisions.
reflections.adaptation_notes: The key adaptation over six ticks has been reframing disruption data as evidence rather than threat. RoboRide adoption, unemployment rising, car owners giving up vehicles — every piece of bad news for the old auto economy is a piece of evidence that the new training pipeline is needed now. I need to hold onto that framing as the April board review approaches and the pressure to be defensive increases. Stay on offense with data. Also: the coalition is more important than the curriculum. The board will fund a program that has community buy-in. My job is to show up with allies, not just a slide deck.

reflections.reflection: Nine ticks. The board review happened this tick — or is happening now — and I walked in with something I could not have built in a week or a month. I built it over nine months of disciplined, sequential decisions, each one adding a layer of credibility the next one depended on. I had Howard Liu's written statement from auto row as a physical document in the folder. I had Sarah Kim confirmed as a guest instructor — not a contact, not a plan, an actual commitment from a working mechanic who will stand in my classroom and show students what diagnostic work looks like on a real EV system. I had Councilmember Santos's endorsement and a named grant pathway. I had RoboRide's own delivery expansion as the central argument — a company operating autonomous vehicles in Millfield's residential streets whose maintenance workforce does not exist yet. None of that evidence was available at tick 0. All of it was built, piece by piece, through specific outreach actions I chose to take rather than defer. The Howard Liu gap is worth naming because I deferred it twice in prior reflections and finally closed it in tick 8. That pattern — identifying the uncomfortable action, reflecting on it without doing it, then finally doing it — is one I want to watch in myself. Reflection without action is just journaling. I came closer to the line than I should have on that one.
reflections.identity_shift: At tick 6 I said I could see the identity of a community institution builder from where I was standing but had not crossed into it yet. I think I have crossed it now. I am not thinking about whether the board funds the program. I am thinking about what the program looks like in five years, whether the community college pipeline is fully formalized, whether Frank Russo's continuing education work and Sarah Kim's guest sessions become a permanent advisory structure rather than informal relationships. The board's decision matters — it matters enormously for the program's near-term survival — but my horizon has extended past it. That is the difference. I am not waiting to see if the program gets saved. I am already building what comes after it.
regrets: I deferred the Howard Liu visit through two full reflection cycles before acting on it. That gap between identifying the right action and taking it is a pattern I need to close faster. In a disruption environment, slow follow-through on known priorities compounds into real cost. I got lucky that the delay did not cost me the statement before the board review.

I have not engaged Carlos Ruiz directly. He is in my network as a master mechanic and his trust score with me is low — 0.36. Sarah Kim has a relationship with him and is navigating her own conversation with him about the RoboRide situation. There may be a version of the program that brings him in as a senior industry voice, but I have not cultivated that relationship. If the board approves the program and the partnership structure deepens, Carlos is someone I need to eventually approach.
successes: The board presentation is the strongest case I have ever made for anything in my professional life. That is not an accident. Every piece of evidence in that presentation was deliberately assembled: the Santos endorsement came from a cold email to her office, the Howard Liu statement came from overcoming my own inertia, Sarah Kim's guest session came from listening to her situation rather than pitching mine. The coalition is real and it is visible in the document.

Savings have grown every tick without exception. Employment is stable at 67% community-wide but my own position is secure, my stress is low, and my financial runway is longer now than when I started. Building under stability is a privilege I have tried to honor by taking actions that extend it rather than trading on it.

Frank Russo is self-organizing. That is the most underrated success of the last nine ticks. I did not create his energy — I just met him at his level, listened without pitching, and let him find the vision himself. He is now contacting continuing education intake on his own initiative. That is what coalition looks like when it is working: people acting in their own interests in ways that happen to build the same infrastructure.
reflections.adaptation_notes: The main adaptation between tick 6 and tick 9 has been moving from coalition-building to coalition-deployment. Building was the right mode for ticks 1 through 8. Ticks 0 through 8 were preparation. Tick 9 is execution. If there is a lesson from the full arc, it is that disruption creates urgency but preparation creates credibility, and credibility is what actually moves institutions. The board is not being asked to take a risk on an untested idea. They are being asked to fund something that already has a city councilmember's endorsement, a parts supplier's written validation, a working mechanic as a confirmed partner, and a peer educator independently advancing the same pipeline. That stack of evidence does not happen without nine ticks of specific, disciplined decisions. Next challenge: if the board approves, the real work begins. Bureaucratic approval is not program success. Enrollment, retention, job placement outcomes, community college articulation agreements — those are the metrics that will matter in six more ticks. I need to start thinking about that infrastructure now, not after the approval is in hand.
